This brief presentation of the **Brahmanic religious system** <note>The author uses this term to describe the complex theological and social structures of Hinduism as understood by European scholars in the late 18th century.</note> was initially intended for the readers of the *Transactions of the Calcutta Scholarly Society* <note>original: "Calcuttischen Gelehrtengesellschaft"; this refers to the Asiatic Society, founded in Calcutta (Kolkata) by Sir William Jones in 1784.</note> and was therefore meant to constitute a part of the fourth volume of the aforementioned work. However, despite the conciseness of the delivery and the removal of anything not strictly necessary for understanding the individual main points of this system or for an overview of the whole, it has grown so substantial that it will constitute a moderate volume on its own. It thus appears under a double title: namely, for the owners of those *Transactions*—to whom this presentation of the Brahmanic religious system will be useful and not unwelcome in more than one respect—as a fourth part of the

aforementioned work; however, all those who do not possess that work, but who might consider this writing worthy of their attention for the sake of the subject matter itself, may obtain it under its own separate title.

With respect to the execution itself and the explained fundamental concepts <term>Grundbegriffe: the foundational principles or ideas that form the basis of a system of thought</term> or the original and peculiar modes of representation <term>Vorstellungsarten: the specific ways a culture perceives, visualizes, and conceptualizes abstract or spiritual ideas</term> that are considered here, perhaps those readers who are at least knowledgeable enough in this subject will feel some gratitude toward the author. They will recognize the difficulties involved in providing a precise and definite account of that without which no true fundamental view of this system <note>The "system" refers to the complex structure of Indian theology and philosophy as analyzed by the author.</note> can be conceived, and how little one can learn in this regard from the common reports concerning the religion and religious superstition of the Indians <note>original: "Indier"; a term used historically to refer to the people of the Indian subcontinent.</note>.

A writing of this kind, if it is to be truly useful and, at least as a whole—

# Preliminary Report.

---

taken as a whole, is to be reliable, it presupposes insights and a power of judgment <term>Beurtheilungskraft: the capacity to critically evaluate and form sound opinions, especially in scholarly contexts</term> such as one can by no means expect from the authors of so many booklets undertaken at random regarding these and other foreign religions. There are uncritical, as well as false and tasteless compilations <term>Compilazionen: works assembled by pulling together various existing texts, often without original research or critical vetting</term> of this kind, which, like so many other things, serve only as proof of the recklessness with which an immature mind today dares to venture into subjects that were not made for him.

Regarding a portion of the contents of this work, there is a small publication that I must mention specifically. Hindostan"; Malabar refers to the southwestern coast of India, while Hindustan was a common historical term for the Indian subcontinent or its northern regions.</note>—in the year 1791 at Berlin (at the Academic Art and Bookstore) pub—

# Preliminary Report. VIII

---

published; <note>original: "gekommen"; completing "herausgekommen" from the previous page</note> I received and compared it, however, only after this work was already completed and dispatched. Its author did not name himself; nor does one find the slightest indication of how, and under what circumstances, it is supposed to have arisen from observations made in Hindustan <term>Hindustan: a historical name for the Indian subcontinent, often used in this period to refer specifically to Northern India</term> itself. Be that as it may, the attentive reader of the present representation of the Brahmanic religious system <term>Brahmanic religious system: an 18th-century scholarly term for Hinduism, emphasizing the role of the Brahmins and the Sanskrit scriptural tradition</term> will be perfectly capable of judging its content. Although, in my judgment, it reveals no thorough insight into the nature and the connection between the parts and concepts of this system, much less provides such insight, most of the statements and explanations in it (insofar as these belong to those whom the anonymous author claims to have consulted orally and in writing) are correct and, on the whole, consistent with the content of older original writings <term>Originalschriften: refers here to primary source manuscripts, likely in Sanskrit or local dialects, as opposed to secondary European accounts</term>. # Preliminary Report. VIII

---

individual <note>original: "nen"; completing "einzelnen" from the previous page</note> explanations of the collector and narrator are concerned, these are only partially well-founded, namely insofar as they concern the external (common legend and fable <note>original: "Sage und Fabel"</note>); on the other hand, many other things are based on misunderstandings. Such errors are quite common—indeed inevitable—when dealing with a religious system like the mythic-allegorical one of the Brahmins <term>Brahmins: the priestly and scholarly class of India, responsible for maintaining sacred knowledge</term>, which deviates so significantly from all European teachings and modes of thought.

Regarding certain individual points, one could have spoken more elaborately and in greater detail; I would have done so for the benefit of those who are little informed about such matters, if the purpose of this work had not been to remain as concise as possible. Nevertheless, nothing has been omitted that seemed necessary to give the reader a true and complete concept of the whole.

<summary>The author explains that many European misunderstandings of Indian religion are inevitable due to the vast differences in worldview, but asserts that his own work provides a complete overview despite its brevity.</summary>
<keywords>Brahmins, religious systems, Indian mythology, European scholarly perspective, interpretation errors, Hinduism</keywords>

# Preliminary Report. IX

The attached copperplates <term>Copperplates: illustrations printed from etched or engraved metal plates, which were the standard for high-quality scientific and artistic reproductions in 18th-century books</term> serve partly as evidence and partly as an explanation of what has been stated. They are all taken from Paullinus’s <note>Pauline of St. Bartholomew (1748–1806) was an Austrian missionary and orientalist who published some of the first European grammars of Sanskrit.</note> *The Brahmanic System* <note>original Latin title: "Systema Brahmanicum"</note>. From the thirty-two copperplates in that work—all of which were engraved based on original Indian artworks preserved in Cardinal Borgia’s <note>Cardinal Stefano Borgia was a famous collector of foreign antiquities; his museum in Velletri was a major center for scholars of non-European cultures.</note> museum in Velletri—the most significant and most useful for our purpose have been selected.

The final plates concerning the four primary Indian alphabets, and the Sanskrit-Malabar script in particular, are from Paullinus’s *Sidharubam* or *Sanskrit Grammar* <note>original Latin title: "Grammatica Samscrdamica"</note>. These belong to the appendix of this work, in which the Sanskrit <note>original: "Sanskritischen oder Samskrdamischen"</note> language is not only discussed in general, but a productive excerpt from the aforementioned writing is also provided, which [serves] to...

->### Preliminary Remarks.<-

The various religions of nations, especially those of antiquity, always present a remarkable subject for reflection and investigation, even from a moral perspective. What they have in common in their manner of expression, and what each possesses uniquely, leads to many important comparisons; but they all prove, at least for those times, a general human need to possess some form of religion. Regarding the symbolic-mythological religious service of the Brahmins <term>Brahmins: The priestly class within the Hindu social and religious hierarchy.</term> in particular, one becomes acquainted through it with certain ancient ways of thinking that are found in the same or a similar manner—and concerning the same subjects of nature and imagination—among the ancient Egyptians, Persians, Chinese, and even among the Jewish Kabbalists; — ways of thinking whose historical-genetic origin still remains unexplained <note>Original: *unaufgeschlossen*, meaning "unopened" or "unlocked," implying the source or root of these ideas hasn't been discovered.</note>.

> ...uncertain report, to have collected the so-called Vedams <term>Vedams: A regional variant of the term "Vedas."</term> of Southern India, and Colonel Polier <note>Antoine-Louis Henri Polier (1741–1795) was a Swiss adventurer and collector of oriental manuscripts in India.</note>, as Jones <note>Sir William Jones (1746–1794), a famous Anglo-Welsh philologist and scholar of ancient India.</note> asserts, possesses in their entirety those Bedas <term>Bedas: Another variant of "Vedas."</term> that are recognized in Bengal. Neither the former nor the latter have become known until now.

->### Preliminary Remarks<-

...here, namely, certain statements and explanations from original writings were taken into account, which one finds with this missionary

---

> [published for] the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith <note>original: "S. Congregationis de P. F." (Sacra Congregatio de Propaganda Fide) — the Vatican department responsible for missionary work.</note> I have already published. Now I present the principal chapters of the Brahmanic Vocabulary, called *Amarasinha* <note>original: "Amarafinha" — a Latinized transcription of Amarasimha, the author of the *Amarakosha*, the most celebrated Sanskrit lexicon.</note>, so that some light may shine upon Indian matters—which until now have lain in long-lasting obscurity—from genuine Brahmanic manuscripts, and so that the fabrications of conjecturers may at long last vanish. — There are, therefore, two primary reasons that drove me to labor over this work. The first: so that, by means of this classic Brahmanic manuscript, the triflers, babblers, busybodies, soothsayers, and the English and French Indian travelers unskilled in the Sanskrit language <note>original: "linguae Samscrdamicae"</note>, as well as other reckless tricksters of Indian affairs, might be corrected, refuted, and chastised; and finally, so that their dreams and follies, with which they have filled all of Europe, might be expelled and scattered. The second: to comply with the Most Eminent Cardinal Borgia <note>Stefano Borgia (1731–1804), a cardinal and antiquarian who founded the Borgia Museum in Velletri.</note>, a man who has served the republic of letters most excellently and is to be heaped with every praise, who was the instigator and a timely guide for me in publishing this little work. 7) Father Paullinus <note>Paulinus a Sancto Bartholomaeo (1748–1806), an Austrian Carmelite missionary and one of the first European scholars to study Sanskrit.</note> writes regarding this (*Sidharubam* p. 74) as follows: <note>The following is translated from the original Latin.</note> "What is commonly said by the Indians is that there are four laws, six sciences, and 18 ancient histories, whether true or legendary. But this popular axiom is false if applied to the Brahmins <term>Brahmins: the priestly and scholarly class in the Indian caste system</term>, for they admit only three laws—namely, the *Irku*, *Sama*, and *Yagiu* <note>original Latin spellings: "Irku, Sáma, Yagiu"; referring to the Rig, Sama, and Yajur Vedas</note>, which taken together are called the *Rig-Sama-Yajur Veda*. The fourth law is a popular one and deals with incantations, sorcery, divinations, and judicial astrology; it pertains not to the Brahmins, but to the Shudras <term>Shudras: the social class traditionally associated with labor and service</term> and other lower tribes.

Whatever is contained in the Brahminical books is distributed into three classes: the *Veda*, the *Shastra*, and the *Purana* <term>Purana: a genre of ancient Indian literature covering myths, legends, and traditional lore</term>. Under the *Veda*, only those books are included which deal with divine worship, such as the precepts concerning sacrifices, prayers, fasts, pilgrimages, and expiations - - - - All of these together are called *Geba homa devaram*. Thus, the Veda is not a single book, as most Europeans think, who so often—yet falsely and ridiculously—have boasted that they found and possessed 'the book of Veda' in India, and of whom more than twenty have [brought] forward..."

# ->Preliminary Remark<-

Adherents of this religion who are best informed about the matter—or believe themselves to be—make a distinction regarding their sacred scriptures between the very first code of laws (or the original religious record) and the explanations of it that arose later. However, in practical terms, little attention is paid to this distinction, the reason for which is very easily recognized from those accounts by **Holwell** <note>John Zephaniah Holwell (1711–1798) was an employee of the East India Company whose works were among the first to introduce Hindu philosophy to Europe, though he often conflated different texts.</note>.

Whether that original religious record still exists, or whether it is merely older explanations and other religious writings bearing the same names that are taken for it (such as, for example, the **Schasta** <note>original: "Schasta"; referring to the *Shastras*.</note>, which was praised to **Holwell** as the oldest religious record and which he himself recognizes as such), it is at least clear from that tradition that the matter itself is not without foundation. It is only to be regretted that these reports originate only from the Ganges and Hindostan <note>A historical term for Northern India, specifically the Indo-Gangetic Plain.</note> proper, without knowing how those writings which are considered the oldest religious scriptures in southern India relate, in terms of their content, to the Sha-

## Brahminical Religious System.

This religion can be viewed either according to the simpler and original teachings of the actual religious documents <note>original: "Religionsurkunden"; in this context, the author refers to the primary scriptures or Vedas.</note>; or according to the infinitely multifaceted, highly complex, mythological-philosophical system of the writings of the second and third rank. It is these latter ones, in fact, upon which the Indian religious teachers <note>original: "Religionslehrer"; likely referring to the Brahmins or Pandits who interpreted the texts for the public.</note> form their entire way of thinking, and which they regard as the foundation and source of all their wisdom and scholarship.

# Section 1. Concerning the Deities

Regarding the actual religious documents <note>original: "Religionsurkunden"; refers to the primary sacred texts or Vedas.</note>, we can thus far judge them only according to the fragments that Holwell <note>John Zephaniah Holwell (1711–1798) was an employee of the East India Company. His writings provided many Europeans with their first, albeit sometimes inaccurate, look at Hindu theology.</note> made known from the so-called Shastra <note>original: "Schasta"; a reference to the Shastras, the authoritative texts of Indian philosophy and law.</note>. These fragments certainly extend across the most important points of the Indians' religious belief; however, there are only a few of them: he lost most of them through shipwreck <note>Holwell claimed his original translations and manuscripts were lost during the Siege of Calcutta in 1756.</note>. I shall make use of them in a manner that will also be justified by other reasons.

By contrast, the theogonic-mythological system that serves as the foundation throughout the writings of the second and third rank <note>likely referring to the Puranas or other secondary commentaries.</note> rests on principles that belong, to a certain extent, to the doctrine of emanation <term>Emanation: the belief that the universe and all beings are not created "out of nothing," but flow out of or radiate from the essence of a single divine source.</term>. The essence of the theory of emanation consists in this:

<margin>18</margin> 1. that the origin and constituent parts of all things are derived from a single, absolutely infinite and incomprehensible Primal and Universal Being <note>original: "Ur- und Allwesen"</note>, by means of the auxiliary concept of eradiations (radiations) or of generations. With the former (the concept of eradiations), there lies the image of light and its properties; with the latter, that of a twofold primal—

<margin>19</margin>The deities of this system are divided into the One Eternal Original Being <note>original: "Urwesen"; a term for the primal source or ultimate reality.</note> and the generated gods with their female halves <note>original: "weiblichen Hälften"; referring to the divine consorts or Shaktis who represent the active power of their respective gods.</note>. According to the explanation of the Brahmin Chandra Govinda <note>original: "Ciandra Govinda"</note>, the spirit and understanding of God is like the light of the moon, which is neither burning nor dark, but always gentle and bright. “Yet it is only a similitude,” he said, “through which the essence of your spirit, O God, is not expressed. You are the true, eternally blessed, immutable light of all times and spaces. Your wisdom recognizes a thousand and more than a thousand laws, and yet you act at all times freely and to your glory. Humans cannot penetrate into your hiddenness, and we ourselves are all—”

<margin>24</margin>After the Primordial Being <note>original: "Urwesen," referring to the absolute, unmanifested deity.</note> or the Eternal One, and its twofold primordial power <note>original: "Urkraft," the creative energy often identified with Shakti.</note>, the three first-begotten gods—Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva—with their female halves, come into consideration. Their character, attributes, and effects, when taken together, are intended to represent the infinite Deity as perceptible, or in the state of its revelation and activity outside of itself. Therefore, the external veneration of the Deity through prayers, sacrifices, and religious customs primarily adheres to these three and has them almost exclusively as its objects. With their female powers, they are, in a sense, three Gnostic syzygies <term>Syzygies: In Gnostic philosophy, these are pairs of male and female divine beings or "aeons" that represent a union of opposites necessary for creation.</term> or unions of a male and female Aeon <term>Aeon: An eternal divine power or being that emanates from the supreme source.</term> into a pair, and indeed they are the first or highest of these pairs.

For this reason, these three are also depicted sitting on a lotus, etc.

# Section 1. On Deities and Sacred Objects

<margin>36</margin> 3. The third pair of the generated deities are Shiva (also Ishvara and Mahadeva) and Parvati or Bhavani. See Table VIII. Fig. 11.

Shiva (called Siew by Holwell <note>John Zephaniah Holwell (1711–1798), an early English employee of the East India Company who wrote extensively on Indian culture</note>, and Seba, Siba, or Siw by others) is the first progression of the primordial male power or fire in the highest sense, and therefore generally bears the character of the Destroyer, Transformer, Avenger, and strict Supreme Judge. ## II. Trimurti. 3) Shiva.

...is, sitting in the middle of his forehead,) and is the "One with Bristling Hair," the Creator, Master of the Mountain, and Ruler of the Three Realms (heaven, earth, and the underworld). He carries the moon or the river Ganges upon his head, creating rain and thunderstorms, and appears as the Bull and as a Hermaphrodite (*Ardhanarishvara* <note>original: "Arthanári"</note>). See Table IX, Figures 12–13.

These names and descriptions, which are recited in sequence every day, reveal his character, which is easily recognizable in various—and at times grotesque—depictions. He is presented sometimes riding a bull, or carrying the Ganges on his forehead; he is armed with a trident and surrounded by snakes, lightning, and skulls. He is even shown splitting children with an axe, though his name literally means "The Good One." He carries the <term>Yoni: a symbol of the womb or female creative energy</term> <note>original: "Joni oder Matrix"</note> and the <term>Lingam: the phallic symbol representing Shiva's generative power</term>, often possessing many arms and displaying several attributes simultaneously. 23)

## II. Trimurti. 3) Shiva.

Parvati <note>original: "Parwadi"</note> or Bhavani, the third of the 38 female emanations <note>the text uses "progressions" to describe how divine energy flows outward into specific forms</note>, shares all the duties of Shiva as his wife and therefore, like her husband, possesses a dual character. Specifically, she is both the benevolent progenitress and giver of joy, as well as the avenger—comparable to the Greek goddesses Hecate <note>goddess of magic and the underworld</note> and Nemesis <note>goddess of retribution</note>.

The lotus, the moon, and the Ganges are her primary symbols. As a benefactress (See Plate X, Fig. 14), she is called "the Good One" (Shivaa) <note>the feminine form of Shiva</note>, the Great Lady and Sovereign, the active power, the life-giving mother, and the commanding creator of joy and well-being. — As an avenger (See Plate XI, Fig. 15), she bears epithets such as "The Tear-Bringer," "The Holy One," "The Black One," and so on. This is because the creations beneath the moon, over which she rules alongside Shiva, are not purely good in their effects, but rather mixed. According to this latter character, she is represented in many temples with wide-open and terrifying eyes, a black face, and long, protruding teeth; she is entwined by snakes and has eight or sixteen arms, armed with a sword, trident, and a vessel for blood, sitting on a wood—

Shrirama <note>Rama, the hero of the Ramayana epic</note>—the sixth incarnation <term>incarnation: the earthly embodiment of a deity</term> of Vishnu—is a young hero of great beauty, equipped with a bow, arrow, and snake, and of a greenish color. According to the **Bhagavata** <note>original: *Bhagaweda*; likely referring to the *Bhagavata Purana*, which details the life of Krishna</note>, **Krishna** was born in **Mathura** <note>original: *Madhu*; located 25 miles from Agra</note>. Thirty-six years after his death, the fourth world-period or **Kali Yuga** began.

### III. Lesser Deities. 4. Krishna.

Paullinus <note>Paulinus a Sancto Bartholomaeo (1748–1806) was an Austrian missionary and early Orientalist who published some of the first European works on Sanskrit and Indian culture.</note> shows \*) that the names of the cities **Panda** and **Madura** (that is, the colony of Madu) occurring among the ancients, as well as the region of the **Pandauon** <note>original Greek: *Πανδαυων*</note>, and **Pandaea**—the only daughter of **Hercules**, from whom the land took its name—fit the fable of **Krishna** and the war of the **Pandavas**. \*) Pliny, *Natural History* 6, 16. 20. 23. Arrian, *The Anabasis of Alexander* I, 1. Ptolemy, *Geography* 7. table 10. <note>These are classical Greco-Roman references used by 18th-century scholars to link Indian geography and myth to the Western tradition.</note>

"Through this," he adds, "the cattle-herding of **Apollo** is explained, <note>original Latin: *quia Sol pascit omnia*</note> because the Sun feeds all things—**Krishna** visited all the women, <note>original Latin: *nempe stellas in coeli latifundio*</note> namely the stars in the vast expanse of heaven, and impregnated them through his light." Therefore, **Krishna** is the black or dark Sun <note>original Latin: *Sol ergo Krshna niger aut fuscus*</note>, because he is deprived of light during an eclipse; he stole butter <note>original Latin: *butyrum furatus est*</note> because he liquefied it with his rays and heat—he is crowned with a flowery wreath <note>original Latin: *floreo serto coronatur*</note> because he is the creator of flowers; he plays the flute <note>original Latin: *fistula canit*</note> because he himself produces the winds; he is joined in marriage to the stars; [and was killed] by his master **Beren** <note>likely referring to the hunter Jara; see previous page</note>, the silent ascetic <note>original Latin: *hesychasta*</note>...

### 2. Of the Luminous Celestial Bodies.

For although it might seem that certain doctrines of thoroughly useful and true content allow for nothing but a good use, while others, conversely, permit only a bad and harmful use—as if nothing bad could be drawn from the former, and nothing good from the latter—yet history and experience, as well as the nature of the matter itself, teach us that the very best of this kind can be abused just as much as the more imperfect can be put to good use. This latter occurs as soon as the interpretation and application of such a doctrine—however imperfect it may be—is guided by a pure need of the heart, or by a good will and a moral sense that is earnest about the truth; the former, on the contrary, occurs when malice, hypocritical falsehood <note>original: "gleißende Falschheit," literally "glittering falsehood," describing a deception that looks beautiful or pious on the surface.</note>, and selfishness lie at the root. <margin>80</margin>The religious teachings of the Brahmanical system <note>The author uses this term to describe the Hindu religious and social order as it was understood by European scholars in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.</note>, which we have most recently explained, may be regarded however one wishes; yet they are by no means so poor that they would not allow for a better and more beneficial use than the Brahmins—taken as a whole—see fit to permit. This priestly caste—just as proud as it is superstitious, and at the same time cunning and selfish—considers itself, on account of Brahma, to be the born head of the human race. They claim for themselves a nobility to which nothing else—not even the highest, noblest, or most meritorious—can ever be compared, for its root is hidden in the brain of Brahma <note>A reference to the Vedic myth of the Purusha, where the Brahmins are said to have been created from the mouth or head of the primordial being, signifying their status as teachers and priests.</note>. **all the incarnations of the god Vishnu are displayed, carved in order into the cliffs, I myself saw and examined in the year 1776.** <note>original Latin: "omnes incarnationes dei Vishnu ex ordine rupibus insculptae exhibentur, ego a. 1776. ipsemet vidi et examinavi." **"Although indeed in the sketching of the human body, and especially in the fashioning of larger statues, there is neither Greek liveliness nor Roman correctness, nevertheless in the painting of smaller figures, in the representation of wars, in the decoration of triumphal chariots and temple facades, the wonderful skill of the Indians shines through—a beautiful and pleasing simplicity, and finally an elegant variety, which certainly has never been seen in ancient Egyptian monuments—"** <note>original Latin: "Quamvis vero in delineando humano corpore... quae certe in antiquis Aegyptiis monumentis nunquam visa fuit"</note>

Whether they were all pagodas? <note>In the 18th and 19th centuries, European writers used the term "pagoda" to refer generally to Hindu temples.</note> — The sight seems to proclaim nothing else: everything that Thévenot <note>Jean de Thévenot (1633–1667), a French traveler who was one of the first Europeans to describe the Ellora caves.</note> and Anquetil <note>Abraham-Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron (1731–1805), a French orientalist.</note> found there led to this idea and only to this one. And yet one might doubt it, insofar as it can hardly be seen what purpose several hundred temples to the gods should serve so close beside and above one another, unless one considers that for a people like the Indians, and a priestly caste like the Brahmins, the creation of a pantheon such as this—in those ancient times of power and religious fervor—could not have seemed too great an undertaking, however gigantic it is in itself and however incomparable to all other monuments of religious antiquity it may always remain. Since it was a residence for all the gods, one can easily imagine that many hundreds, perhaps some thousands, of high and low priests would have had their dwellings here at the same time. Now, perhaps, naked Indian holy men or <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>From the Greek for "naked philosophers"; a term used by Western scholars since antiquity to describe Indian ascetics (sadhus) who practiced renunciation and nudity.</note> stay there...

66) <note>original: French</note> What makes this pagoda—which is a grand edifice—the most significant and the foremost in India <note>original: "Indes"</note>, is that it is situated upon the Ganges <note>As noted on the previous page, early European writers often mistakenly associated the Jagannath Temple in Odisha with the Ganges river system</note>; for the idolaters <note>A historical term used by European writers to describe practitioners of non-Abrahamic religions, such as Hinduism</note> believe that the waters of this river possess a particular virtue, and that by bathing there, they are cleansed of their impurities. Moreover, what makes this pagoda so wealthy (for it maintains as many as 20,000 cows) is the vast quantity of alms given there every day by the incredible multitude of people who arrive from all directions. However, these alms are not left so much to the discretion of those who give them, but are rather at the disposal of the High Priest <note>original: "Grand-Prêtre"</note>. Before granting permission to the pilgrims to shave themselves, to bathe in the Ganges, and to perform the other necessary rites to fulfill their vows, he taxes each person according to their means, having strictly informed himself of their status. In this way, he collects immense sums from which he does not take a personal profit; instead, everything is applied to the feeding of the poor and the maintenance of the pagoda. The High Brahmin <note>original: "Grand-Bramin"</note> thus arranges for the necessary provisions to be distributed to the pilgrims every day—such as butter, milk, rice, and flour—but to the poor who lack the utensils to cook their own food, it is given to them already prepared. — — — The revenues of this pagoda are sufficient to provide food every day for fifteen or twenty thousand pilgrims, as such a number is often found there, this pagoda being the place...

<header>2. Sacrifices. 1) Yagna or Yagnam.</header>
<sig>K 2</sig>

This category includes the sacrifices offered to the sun and the planets, to fire, to the deceased, to the ambiguous spirits <note>The original German "zweydeutigen Genien" likely refers to the *Bhutas* or elemental spirits</note>, and to the Lingam <note>A symbolic representation of the god Shiva</note>. These rituals are known by the names Yagna, Homa, Thuka, Pitru-yajna, and Bhuta-yajna (or all these words with the appended neuter "m," such as Yagnam, Homam, and so on).

<margin>98</margin>
1. The sacrifice known as Yagna or Yagnam relates to the sun and the nine planets or celestial spheres <note>The *Navagraha*, or nine celestial influencers in Hindu cosmology</note>. It is a burnt offering <note>original: "Brandopfer"</note>, and is therefore extraordinary in its very nature, considering that the Brahmins otherwise hold a profound reverence for every breath of life <note>A reference to *ahimsa*, the principle of non-violence toward all living things</note>. Its purpose is to obtain a sacred fire that can be used to light the funeral pyres of deceased Brahmins. This ensures that the deceased—exempted from all further purifications within the planetary spheres—may pass directly from their ashes into the state of the glory of Brahma <note>This suggests a belief in a shortcut to *moksha*, or liberation, bypassing the usual cycle of rebirth or intermediate celestial stages</note>.

<margin>99</margin>
Because of its perceived high spiritual purpose, this sacrifice requires extensive preparations. One hundred Brahmins of the more learned class are chosen; they must select a site in a wide, open field, the ground of which must then be prepared according to all four

<header>2. Sacrifice. 4) Pitra Yajna.</header>

4) To promote atonement <gloss>expiation</gloss> and the swifter purification of the soul of the deceased, a sacrifice is offered by their closest relatives, which bears the name **Pitra Yajna** <note>original: *Pidrajagna*; from the Sanskrit *pitr* (ancestor) and *yajna* (sacrifice)</note>, particularly on the anniversaries of their death, and on several other days designated for praying and sacrificing for the departed, and

> an expiatory sacrifice <note>original: *piatorium sacrificium*</note>, called **Thookam** <note>original: *tùkam*; a ritual involving suspension by hooks</note>, is usually offered, in which a certain man is suspended by two hooks inserted into his loins and is carried with great pomp around her shrine. The falling blood, flowing from this man’s wounds, is mixed with the blood of a rooster and, cast into the fire before the altar of this goddess—along with sacred wood—is sacrificed and burned. From which, surely, 1) you may safely infer that in antiquity, human victims were sacrificed to this goddess for the expiation of the people's sins. You may infer 2) that the goddesses **Bhagavati** and **Gangadevi**, otherwise known as **Durga**, are one and the same person. You may infer 3) that in the Brahmanical books, traces of the ancient cult are most certainly found even today, and that this modern cult does not differ from the ancient one as much as Father Georgius, Mr. de Pauw, and Sonnerat—led by I know not what meager arguments—believed. For if indeed that suspended man is not actually slaughtered, it is not to be ascribed to the system of **metempsychosis** <note>original: *metempsychoseos*; the transmigration of souls or reincarnation</note>, which is very ancient and has always prevailed among the **Brahmins**, but rather to the nation, the ritual, and the passage of time, which makes all things milder.

<header>2. Sacrifice. 5) Bhuta Yajna.</header>
L 2

In honor of the wandering night spirits and evil genii <note>from the Latin *genius*; refers to guardian spirits or supernatural beings</note>, among which snakes are also counted, as they are in the *Zend-Avesta* <note>the primary collection of sacred texts of Zoroastrianism</note>, certain stones are consecrated and erected under a small hut. This is done so that the spirits might remain fixed there, without it occurring to them to visit houses and gardens. Often, a light is also placed there for them at night. In Malabar <note>the southwestern coast of India</note>, where the dangerous <term>Kuttichathans</term> <note>mischievous or malevolent spirits in Kerala folklore</note> are said to appear, one places a stone in the gardens of those to whom one wishes ill; through certain magic formulas, one binds an evil demon to it,

whose leader is said to be **Shukra** <note>the regent of the planet Venus</note>, just as **Brihaspati** <note>the regent of the planet Jupiter</note> is the leader of the **Devas** <note>original: *Dévaquel*; referring to the assembly of divine and good spirits</note>. Paullinus <note>Paulinus of St. Bartholomew, a contemporary missionary and scholar of Indian culture</note> believes that all these genii belong to astronomy <note>original: *hos spiritus seu genios bonos malosque ad astronomiam, ad coelestem mundum, ad planetarum phaenomena, referendos esse* — "that these spirits or genii, both good and bad, are to be related to astronomy, the celestial world, and the phenomena of the planets"</note>, though this can hardly apply to all of them. The Indians share this belief in a vast number of good and evil genii with many other nations, who were led to this idea not first, nor solely, by observing the planets, but by many other observations regarding the partly beneficial and partly harmful effects of natural forces, etc.

The Brahmins have declared the destruction of houses of God and those places where penitent religious men live to be one of the gravest and most unpardonable crimes; they do this to protect themselves against rulers who might otherwise take it into their heads to dissolve monasteries.

The Brahmins would by no means cleanse him of his sins until he resolved—after offering many sacrifices that brought the priests no small profit, as they are indispensable to such rites—to pass through a golden cow <note>This refers to the *Hiranyagarbha* ("golden womb") ceremony, a ritual of rebirth and purification where a ruler would literally crawl through a hollow gold statue of a cow or a lotus.</note> which he was required to have specially made. He did so, and this statue stands as a splendid monument of this royal atonement <note>original Latin: "luculentum huius regiae expiationis monumentum"</note>—

<margin>119</margin> The second fasts, under the name **Egaschi** <note>Transliteration of *Ekadashi*, the eleventh lunar day of each lunar fortnight in the Hindu calendar, traditionally observed as a day of fasting.</note>, consist of two days, of which one is the eleventh day after each full moon, and the other is the eleventh after each new moon. Until sunset, one abstains from all nourishment to such an extent that not even a **betel leaf** <term>betel leaf</term> <note>The leaf of the *Piper betle* plant, often chewed in South Asia for its stimulant effects.</note> may be chewed.

From what we have said thus far regarding the objects of the **Brahmanical religion** <note>A term used by 18th and 19th-century scholars to describe the religious system of India, now generally referred to as Hinduism.</note> and the manner of worshipping them, it is easy to see what is to be thought of the value and lack of value of this religion, which, taken as a whole, is very ancient. ### 2nd Section. On external relations and so forth.

no people cling so stubbornly to their religion and their customs as the Indians, that their abhorrence of the practices and habits of other peoples is indescribable; that especially the Brahmins and ascetics <note>The original "Büßer" (penitents) refers here to Hindu sadhus or practitioners of extreme self-discipline.</note> have an insurmountable aversion to everything European; that the Mughals oppress and plague them indescribably, yet they far prefer this yoke to a more comfortable and peaceful life offered to them by the European factories <note>In this period, "factories" were not manufacturing plants but coastal trading posts and merchant colonies.</note>; that one could devastate their lands just as horribly as the Mughals, inflict all imaginable cruelties upon them, and whip them with iron rods under the yoke of servitude, but one will never bring them to the point of denying their gods;—that no missionary has ever converted a Brahmin, but only some of the most despised people from the lowest rank, whom misery had made indifferent to their religion, whereas a Brahmin, who believes himself far superior to all kings, will never consent to make himself equal to a Pariah <note>Historically used to refer to those outside the four main castes, often subjected to severe social exclusion.</note> by adopting the Christian religion, and so forth. Furthermore, Sonnerat is right to say that the heathens of India have hitherto perhaps become slaves, but never proselytes <note>People who have converted from one religion or opinion to another.</note> of foreign nations.

These four classes, castes, tribes, or lineages—which are divided into 88 individual sub-classes based on the differences of their specific destiny and individual duties—are fundamentally distinct and forever separated from one another. ### Section 3. Regarding the Caste of the Brahmins.

Among their privileges is the fact that everything concerning religion and the interpretation of the law belongs exclusively to them. They alone are permitted to read the actual religious scriptures and make decisions based upon them. To obey them blindly, to revere them with superstitious devotion, and to bestow upon them abundant gifts belongs, according to their claims, to the most necessary and meritorious works of the non-Brahmins. They cannot be punished by death, but can only be declared to have forfeited their status and be banished—and this only by fellow Brahmins. They are also the regular advisors to kings.

The Brahmins alone wear this ceremonial sash by right; the second caste <note>The *Kshatriyas* or warriors</note> wears it by permission, and others wear it through misuse.

The initiation occurs as follows:

The **Guru** exhorts the prospective **Sanyasi** <term>Sanyasi: a religious mendicant who has renounced all worldly attachments</term> to penance and to the fulfillment of the duties of this final stage. In the presence of many praying **Brahmins**, the Guru performs the **homa** <term>homa: a sacred ritual involving offerings into a consecrated fire</term> sacrifice. He is stripped of his clothing and receives a piece of yellow cloth, which he puts on while reciting prayers. He is forbidden from entrusting this cloth to anyone else for washing; he must wash it himself. These knots serve as a reminder of the seven Great Rishis <note>original: "Muni"</note> or "Hesychasts" <term>Hesychast: a term borrowed from Greek Christian mysticism meaning "one who seeks inner stillness," used here by the author to describe the Great Sages</term> (**Mahà Irushi** <note>Maharishis: the seven primary sages of Hindu tradition</note>). <margin>157</margin> Over their shoulder, the **Sanyasis** usually wear a tiger skin, much like **Shiva** <note>original: "Schiwa"</note>, the avenger of all evil and the subduer of all monsters. They place this skin beneath them when they sleep or use it as a covering.

They never cook their own meals but live solely on alms. They receive these either by silently extending their hand to passersby or those standing in doorways, or by living in a temple, mute and motionless, where they allow the **Brahmins** to bring them rice, fruit, and similar food. When they enter a home, everyone casts themselves at their feet, as do those who visit them when they remain stationary in a single place.

<margin>158</margin> A Sanyasi <term>Sanyasi: a Hindu ascetic who has renounced all worldly life and social ties</term> no longer visits temples or holy places; he does not offer sacrifices, nor does he attend fixed and holy rituals, for he no longer requires these external means. He allows his nails to grow as long as they will; some shave their beard and head, while others never do; some anoint themselves with oils, others do not. None among them chew betel <note>a common stimulant in South Asia; its renunciation signifies a turning away from social pleasures</note>, and none wear a sacred mark <note>original: "Charakter"; referring to the tilaka or sectarian forehead mark</note> on their forehead; they only rub their forehead and chest with the ash of cow dung after their bath, which they take three times a day. Their contemplation, so the Brahmins say, is never directed toward anything created or visible, but toward God himself, and purely toward God and his infinite essence, **Parabrahma** <term>Parabrahma: the Supreme Reality or the absolute spirit that transcends all existence</term>.

<margin>159</margin> Their primary endeavor is to elevate themselves to a perfect mastery over all emotions and to overcome all desires, such as sensuality, anger, greed, pride, vindictiveness, etc.

No one weeps over their death, because they are considered to be supremely blessed, as they go directly into the true heaven without ever returning <note>this refers to the concept of Moksha, or liberation from the cycle of reincarnation</note>. They are buried in a sitting position with their feet and hands folded, in a pit filled all around with salt <note>salt is used in these burials to preserve the body and signifies purity</note>.

For the non-Brahmanic castes—among which there are also those who believe themselves called to a religious life of penance—there exist institutions similar to those of the Brahmans. However, these are dismissively called "external sects" by the Brahmanic orders, even though they perform the same rituals and, indeed, carry their penances much further than the Brahmans do. ...fourth caste, or the so-called **Shudra** <term>Shudra: the fourth and lowest of the traditional Hindu social classes (varnas), historically consisting of laborers and artisans</term>. ### Section 3. On the Lineages of the Brahmins <note>While the header refers to Brahmins, the text on this page continues the discussion of the warrior caste's military structures, likely as a transitional section or comparative study.</note>

...of the. <note>This fragment completes a sentence from the previous page, likely "of the country."</note> The ancient Indian battle order <term>Schlachtordnung; the tactical arrangement of troops for combat</term> consisted of elephants, chariots, cavalry <note>original: *Reuter*, riders</note>, and infantry, which, as one can see from a diagram provided by Paullinus <note>Paulinus a Sancto Bartholomaeo (1748–1806), an Austrian missionary and renowned early Indologist</note>, were arranged in a somewhat strange manner. However, it is remarkable that the successive ranks increased according to the ratio of a geometric progression, where the common ratio <note>original: *Exponent*</note> is three.

So in the first rank (**patti**) <note>The smallest unit of the ancient Indian military system</note> stood one elephant, one chariot, three horses, and five infantrymen;

in the second (**Sénamugham**) <note>Sanskrit: *Senamukha*</note>: 3 elephants, 3 chariots, 9 horses, 15 infantrymen;

in the third (**Gutmam**) <note>Sanskrit: *Gulma*</note>: 9 or (3 x 3) elephants, 9 = 3 x 3 chariots, 27 = 3 x 9 horses, 45 = 3 x 15 infantrymen;

in the fourth (**Ganam**) <note>Sanskrit: *Gana*</note>: 27 = 3 x 9 elephants, 27 = 3 x 9 chariots, 81 = 3 x 27 horses, 135 = 3 x 45 infantrymen;

in the fifth (**Váhini**): 81 = 3 x 27 elephants, 81 = 3 x 27 chariots, 243 = 3 x 81 horses, 405 = 3 x 135 infantrymen;

in the sixth (**Vrdana**) <note>Likely a transcription of the Sanskrit *Pritana*</note>: 243 = 3 x 81 elephants, 243 = 3 x 81 chariots, 729 = 3 x 243 horses, 1215 = 3 x 405 infantrymen.

### Section 3. Of the Lineages of the Brahmins <note>While the chapter heading refers to Brahmins, this specific page focuses on the second caste, the Kshatriyas or warriors.</note>

<margin>170</margin> Since this caste of kings and warriors in India has always had its own special fields and landed estates—which was also the case among the ancient Egyptians and Persians—an Indian army was formerly just as easy to assemble as it was to maintain. For everyone had to provide for their own support, as is still the case today among the Marathas <note>The Maratha Empire was a powerful confederacy in India known for its military prowess</note>. A single summons brought together a countless army, just as is still done today among the Tatars and all those peoples from whom the Europeans received the feudal system <term>feudal system: a social structure where land is held in exchange for military service</term>. Their weapons—namely bow and arrow, lance, shield, and sword, etc. etc.—they always kept in readiness, and after the military campaign was completed, everyone returned to their own hearth. 

The Indian kings only began to maintain standing soldiers <note>standing soldiers: a permanent professional army that remains active during peacetime, unlike a citizen militia</note> in more recent times, since foreign peoples—Tatars and Europeans—have flooded India. These soldiers, however, are taken from the third and fourth castes <note>the Vaisyas (farmers/merchants) and Sudras (laborers)</note>, because the lineage of the actual warriors—even if they were willing to accept service for pay <term>Lohndienst: professional military service performed for wages rather than feudal obligation</term>—has for the most part, and indeed here and there entirely, died out. ...partly in the irregular way of life of this class of people.

The Kshatriyas <note>the warrior and ruling caste, second in the traditional social hierarchy of India</note>, you see, do not enter into any formal marriage, but rather they associate, as long as it pleases them, only with a concubine <note>original: *Beyschläferinn*; here referring to a partner in a non-binding union</note>, whom they visit in her house without taking her into their own. She, on her part, is just as little bound: she ends the union as soon as it pleases her and enters into another. She gives her consent by actually accepting and putting on a shirt offered to her by the man desiring her company. The father does not concern himself with the children at all; instead, they remain with the mother and do not inherit from the father, but always from the mother’s brother, just as the father is inherited by the sons of his sister. <note>This describes a matrilineal system of inheritance known as *Marumakkattayam*, historically practiced by the Nayar and certain royal families in Kerala.</note>

A king, therefore, has no actual wife; instead, his sister holds that position, and her sons follow him in government. The eldest of these is called the second king. The royal children <note>the biological children of the king</note> may, however, demand support, but they are not permitted to claim their father’s rank nor pass themselves off as princes.

95) <note>original Latin: *Haec institutio hodiedum in Academia Triciuricensi...*</note> This institution still prevails today in the Academy of Trichur in Malabar, where the form of the ancient native religion remains preserved and intact under native kings. This is in contrast to the northern parts of India, where the original Indian constitutions, religion, customs, and laws were overturned, corrupted, mixed, and violated by the Tartars <note>Likely referring to the Mughal Empire and other Central Asian Islamic dynasties.</note>, Arabs, and the English. — — — From this came the overthrow of the Indian nation and that horrendous devastation of the most fertile soil; towns exhausted by forced labor, tributes, and exactions; violent empires, coerced obedience, and the governance of peoples not according to the prescription of laws, but by arbitrary and blind impulse, so that whatever pleases the ruler is permitted. 

I have seen these things more than once, and I marveled at the "accursed hunger for Indian gold" <note>original Latin: *Indici auri sacra fames*; a play on Virgil's *Aeneid* regarding the corrupting power of greed.</note> which especially torches the Europeans. ### Section 3. Of the Lineages of the Brahmins.

This tax is somewhat large and would appear disproportionate as a standard land tax (<term>Grundsteuer</term>). ### Section 3. Of the Lineage of the Brahmins <note>original: "Von d. Geschl. der Brahm." While the header mentions Brahmins, the text continues the previous page's discussion of the Shudra caste's internal divisions.</note>

Doctors, weavers, manufacturers, garland makers, soothsayers, sorcerers or charmers <note>original: "Besprecher"; those who perform rituals or heal through spoken incantations</note> etc.

All these are divided into guilds <term>Guilds (Zünfte): Professional associations that regulated trades, maintained quality standards, and provided social support for their members.</term>, which have their own leaders who, together with the senior masters, are the regular judges of everything concerning the guild. If matters are questionable or of particular importance, the entire guild must assemble, as the decision is then made by a majority of votes. A primary duty of these leaders is to watch over the rights <term>Rights (Gerechtsame): The specific legal privileges, traditional standing, or jurisdictions belonging to a particular group or guild.</term> of their guild, to settle family disputes among their members, to provide dowries for poor girls of the guild from the communal treasury, to confirm marriages among guild members or, in case of necessity, to grant divorces, and to punish all kinds of offenses that are not too severe. In short, every guild governs itself and has its own administration of justice; only when an expulsion from the guild and caste is decreed is it reported to the King, so that through the authority of the highest public power that extreme punishment may be carried out, and an outcast of this kind may be sold as a slave. The money given for this falls into the King's treasury.

4. Aside from the four noble and laudable castes described thus far, there exists yet another impure and abhorred one, known as the **Parejas** or **Pariahs**, and also **Palejas**. ### Section 3. On the Lineages of the Brahmins.

Abhorrence toward these people knows no bounds. They live in wretched huts, which must be quite far removed from all cities and villages so that their atmosphere does not "infect" others. # General Overview

<margin>185</margin> One can, as previously noted, consider this religion partly according to the simpler and original teachings of the actual religious documents <term>Religionsurkunden: primary sacred texts or foundational scriptures</term>; and partly according to the much more diverse and complicated theological-philosophical or mytho-theological systems of the writings of the second and third rank. This latter system rests on principles which, to a certain extent, belong to the theory of emanation <note>Emanation theory suggests that all things flow from a single, divine source, becoming less "divine" as they move further away from that source.</note>, the essence of which consists in the following:

1.  that all plurality of existing things is derived from the unity of an absolute being, by means of the auxiliary concepts of radiations <note>original: "Ausstrahlungen"</note> or generations;

2.  that everything existing is interrelated, so that the same properties belong to entirely different beings according to their essence and kind, though not according to their degree;

3.  that all irradiations <note>original: "Eradiazionen"</note> or progressive generations are considered according to the analogy of a number series or numerical progression (Nos. 17—18).

### General Overview

The second section, concerning the nature <margin>193</margin> and the means of external religious service according to this system, begins with several remarks on the abuse to which religious doctrines in general are subjected, and on the self-interest of the **Indian priests**. These priests, instead of applying the simpler and original fundamental teachings of their religion in a way beneficial to the people, have instead ruled them for millennia through ignorance, distressing superstition, **idolatry** <gloss>image worship</gloss>, and hypocritical pretenses (R. 79-83).

### Sanskrit Grammar.

[Sanskrit] <note>Completing the word *Samskrdamische* from the previous page.</note>, which we might simply call Malabaric, must be very ancient because very old inscriptions are found in it (p. 8). However, I would not go so far as to claim that it is the original script in which the oldest writings of the **Brahmins** <note>The priestly and scholarly class of Hindu society, responsible for the preservation of sacred texts.</note> were first composed. Furthermore, those four **alphabets** <note>Referring to the four scripts discussed: Devanagari, Telinganian (Telugu), Grandonic/Grantha, and Sanskrit-Malabaric.</note> correspond so closely in terms of the order and meaning of the letters that one may rightly conclude they share a common origin. Even the individual character strokes, though they deviate quite noticeably, do not differ so fundamentally that they could not all be traced back to common original features from and according to which they have been modified. In this regard, the **Telinganian** <note>The Telugu script.</note>, as well as the **Nagarian** <note>The Devanagari script, today the most common script for writing Sanskrit.</note>, seem simpler and less elaborate than the **Sanskrit-Malabaric**, although the latter are the most elegant.

The 53 or 54 **radical letters** <term>radical letters: the basic, uncombined consonants and vowels that form the foundation of the writing system</term> of this alphabet can be increased to ten thousand composite characters and more. The missionary **Ildefonso a Presentatione** <note>A Spanish Carmelite missionary (1743–1806) who worked in the Malabar region and studied local languages.</note> has already listed 8,004 of them in his manuscript codex <note>original: *Cod. MS.*</note> (p. 7).

<margin>205</margin> From the name **Grantham**, that is, **book-** or **written language**, as the Sanskrit language is sometimes called (from *Grantha*, meaning palm leaves, and *Grantham* as a neuter term for books consisting of palm leaves), the Tamils have created **Kirendam**, because their alphabet lacks characters for the Sanskrit sounds *gr* and *nth*.

The true name of that language, however, according to the **Amarasimha** <note>Referring to the *Amarakosha*, the famous Sanskrit lexicon compiled by the scholar Amarasimha.</note>, is **Samskrda**, in which the *am* is pronounced through the nose <note>A description of the *anusvara*, the nasalized vowel sound in Sanskrit.</note>. With the addition of the Malabar <note>The author uses "Malabar" to refer to the Malayalam language or the regional dialect of the southwest coast of India.</note> neuter ending *m*, it becomes **Samskrdam**.

This name is composed of the two words **Sam**, meaning **together** <note>original: *samt*, in connection, *iunctim*</note>, and **Krda**, meaning something **perfected**, or precisely **ordered** <note>original: *res perfecta, accurate disposita*</note>. They are joined by means of the *s* as an auxiliary letter, which is very frequently used when two or more words are joined to form a compound. **Samskrda** therefore means, according to our author, as much as something precisely **ordered** and thoroughly **perfect** or **complete**. [This] **surname Samskrdam** <note>The author is referring to the name "Sanskrit" as an epithet or descriptive title rather than a primary name.</note> leads one to easily see that it was not original—that is, it was not named after the people or the land by and in which this language was first spoken. **Sidha** or **Sidham**, the grasping and retaining in the soul.

The northern Indians call the grammar of the scholarly language ***Saraswad*** (***Sarasvada***), or according to Cassianus Beligattius <note>Cassian Beligatti (1708–1791), an Italian Capuchin missionary who authored works on the alphabet and languages of India and Tibet</note> ***Suoarasot***, that is, the art of speaking correctly and harmoniously. ***Sarasa*** is harmony and <note>original: "res ad regulam et gustum facienda"</note> "a thing to be fashioned according to rule and taste," while ***Wada*** means expression or <note>original: "dictio"</note> speech. ***Saraswada*** <note>Saraswati</note> is also the name for the wife of Brahma, as the goddess of harmony and of languages.

# Sanskrit Grammar

The sounds *da, dha, ta, tha* cannot be precisely represented by European letters, as their pronunciation varies in hardness or softness depending on whether they appear at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of a word.

This alphabet, which otherwise possesses so many characters for consonants, nonetheless lacks—as do all Indian alphabets—a symbol for *f* or *phi* <note>original: "$\phi$"</note> because this sound does not occur in the language. This is despite how essential that sound is in all older and newer European languages, as well as in several Oriental languages, to which it gives a certain charm. According to the Indian alphabets, one could only write, for example, *factum* <note>Latin: "done"</note>, *fictum* <note>Latin: "invented"</note>, *favor* <note>Latin: "favor"</note>, *fuit* <note>Latin: "he/she/it was"</note>, *Philipp*, and *Feder* <note>German: "feather" or "pen"</note> as *pactum, pictum, pavor, puit, Pilipp,* and *Peder*. The Sanskrit *ph* is indeed not an *f* or *phi* <note>original: "$\phi$"</note>, but rather *p'ha* <note>an aspirated "p" sound, like the "p-h" in "up-hill"</note>.

Among the vowel signs, in addition to the ten characters for *a, e, i, o, u*—both short and long—there are eight more for *rŭ, rû, ilŭ, ilû, am, âh* and the diphthongs <note>complex vowel sounds</note> *ai* or *ei* and *au* <note>original: "äu"</note>, which are treated here entirely as vowels. This arrangement reveals a time when the distinction between the true vowels and the sounds *ru, lu*, <term>etc.</term> <note>original abbreviation "2c." (et cetera)</note> had not yet been observed. The diphthongs *ai* or *ei* and *au*

<margin>215</margin> What makes learning to read so difficult, however, is that:

1. The actual vowel signs are only used at the beginning of a word, never in the middle or at the end of it. If vowels, diphthongs <note>complex vowel sounds</note>, *ru* and *lu*, <term>etc.</term> <note>original abbreviation "2c." (et cetera)</note> are to be expressed here, it is done through entirely different strokes that bear no resemblance to those root signs. These strokes are written above or below the consonants, or are attached directly to them. This, in turn, occurs in various ways depending on the specific consonant. # Sanskrit Grammar

The standard vowel signs are not always placed, which would otherwise very often serve to help one recognize the beginning of a new word. Instead, when a word ends with a consonant and the following word begins with a vowel, the sign for that ending vowel is attached to the consonant of the preceding word, rather than using the standard vowel sign that should have been placed before it. As a result, three or four words can look like a single one. <note>This refers to the phonetic rules of 'Sandhi' and the way Sanskrit script clusters words together without spaces, which can be very confusing for beginners.</note>

From this, there arise:

2. Entirely distinct characters for the vocalized consonants, namely for *kâ*, *kĭ*, *kî*, *kŭ*, *kû*, *kr*, *krû*, *krü*, *kilü*, *kîlu*, *kĕ*, *kai* or *kei*, *cŏ*, *cau*, *cam*, *kah*;
*k'hâ*, *k'hĭ*, *k'hî*, and so forth through all 38 consonants. This results in over 600 specific characters <note>These are known as 'Aksharas' or syllables; because every consonant-vowel combination has a unique shape, the alphabet is much larger than the Western ABCs.</note> with which one must become well-acquainted. The short *ă* is never expressed in the middle or at the end of words; instead, it is pronounced automatically as a <term>native and inherent sound</term> <note>original Latin: "sonus nativus und inhaerens"</note> with every consonant that does not carry another vowel sign.

### II. Excerpt from Friar Paulinus of St. Bartholomew <note>Original: "Fr. Paul. a. S. Barthol." refers to Paulinus a Sancto Bartholomaeo (1748–1806), a Carmelite monk who published some of the first Sanskrit grammars in Europe.</note>

The number of special characters is multiplied even further, making the process of learning to read even more difficult for the beginner:

3. By the vast quantity of signs for compound consonants, where two or three are joined together into a single primary character using shortened and modified strokes. In these cases, the consonant that must be pronounced first is called the <term>regnant</term> <note>original Latin: "regens", meaning the "ruling" or leading consonant in the cluster.</note>, and the other is called the <term>direct</term> <note>original Latin: "recta", referring to the "straight" or governed consonant.</note>. Thus, there are:

a) specific characters for *kra*, *khra*, *gra*, *ghra*, and so on. <note>The apostrophe in the original (k’h) denotes an aspirated sound, where the consonant is followed by a strong puff of air.</note>
b) specific ones for *kla*, *khla*, *gla*, *ghla*, etc.
c) specific ones for *kya*, *khya*, *gya*, *ghya*, etc. <note>The original German uses "j" to represent the "y" sound.</note>
d) specific ones for *kuva* or *kva*, *khuva* or *khva*, etc.
e) specific ones for the <term>governed consonants combined with the letter r</term> <note>original Latin: "consonantes rectae per litteram r"</note> such as *rka*, *rkha*, *rga*, *rgha*, and so on.
f) specific ones for doubled consonants or those joined with <term>final letters</term> <note>original Latin: "litteris finalibus"</note>, such as *kka*, *kkha*, *gga*, *ggha*, etc.
g) specific characters—and indeed in great quantity—for various other combinations, such as: *kda*, *khda*, *kdi*, *kdru*, *kttha*, *gniu*, *gddha*, *ggdhiya*, *ersha*, *rksha*, and so on.

### Supines and Gerunds

*bavidum*, to exist, so that it may be <note>original Latin: *ad existendum, vt sit*</note>.

### Gerund from the First Future

| masculine | feminine | neuter |

The remaining forms of the conjugation are easy to grasp based on the basic form presented so far.

This language has, besides the <term>common verbs</term> <note>original Latin: *verbis communibus*</note>—which may be active, passive, or deponent—also <term>anomalous verbs</term>, some of which carry a passive ending but possess an active meaning. It also includes <term>volitive verbs</term> <note>known in modern linguistics as the desiderative mood</note>, such as *bub'daschti*, "he desires to be" <note>original Latin: *amat esse*</note>, such that the nouns derived from them carry this same pregnant meaning, like "the will to read," etc. There are also <term>frequentative verbs</term>, such as *bob'dajade*, "he is repeatedly" <note>original Latin: *iterum iterumque est*</note>; and <term>causative verbs</term> <note>original: *effectiva*</note>, such as *bâvajadi*, "he causes [something] to exist" <note>original Latin: *facit vt existat*</note>, and so on.

<summary>This page concludes the conjugation of the Sanskrit verb "to be," detailing neuter participles and gerunds before describing the various functional classes of verbs such as causatives and desideratives.</summary>

### II. Extract from Friar Paulinus a S. Bartholomaeo

Regarding **syntax**, there is just as much variety and freedom here in terms of word arrangement as there is in Latin; likewise, in respect to the <term>governance of cases</term> <note>original Latin: *regimen casuum*; this refers to the grammatical rules where certain verbs or prepositions "govern" or require the noun to be in a specific case, such as the dative or accusative.</note>, the Sanskrit language <note>original: *Samskrdamische*</note> bears a great resemblance to Latin.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical index, specifically detailing the entry for Brahma. It follows the previous page's introduction of "Brahm" (the Primal Spirit) by distinguishing it from the personified creator deity Brahma and addressing his iconography, mythology, and various scholarly theories of the time.</meta>

<header>Brah —</header>
<sig>X</sig>

**Brahma**, is conceived in the image of a great man; the same.

— rules and governs over everything in the world; the same.

— has four heads, rides upon a swan, and sits upon the lotus; <note>The swan (*Hamsa*) represents spiritual discernment, while the lotus symbolizes purity and the seat of divine consciousness.</note>

— is, like most deities, a hermaphrodite, and is depicted as such. 27. 28. <note>original: "Hermophrodit." This refers to the concept of the divine containing both masculine and feminine principles, often represented in the form of *Ardhanarishvara*.</note>

— currently has neither temples nor a public cult specifically dedicated to him, though he formerly had both. 29. <note>In Hindu tradition, Brahma is rarely the object of primary worship compared to Vishnu or Shiva, which the author notes as a historical shift.</note>

— when he created the visible world, he floated upon a betel leaf and acted by the power of the spirit that animated him. 73. <note>This likely refers to a variation of the creation myth where the deity floats on the primordial waters; typically, a banyan leaf is cited in Vedic texts, but here the author specifies a betel leaf.</note>

— the Brahmins, who derive their origin from his head, worship him especially every morning. <note>The Brahmins are the priestly caste; according to the *Purusha Sukta*, they were created from the head of the cosmic being.</note>

— He contends with **Vishnu** for primacy, but neither is able to fathom the secret of their origin. 30. <note>original: "Prismat," likely a typesetter's error for "Primat" (primacy). This refers to the myth of the *Lingodbhava*, where Brahma and Vishnu attempt to find the ends of a pillar of fire.</note>

— Great difference between him and the Primal Spirit; <note>The author distinguishes between *Brahma* (the personified creator god) and *Brahman* (the absolute, impersonal "Urgeist" or Primal Spirit).</note>

— he is a purely poetic being, and his mythical character is found in most ancient religions;

— is neither **Abraham**, nor a merely human legislator of India, nor the sun or the earth alone, nor a mere personification of creative power. 31. <note>The author is refuting contemporary European theories, such as those of Thomas Hyde, which attempted to link the Hindu Brahma to the biblical Abraham based on linguistic similarities.</note>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical index, moving from the physical attributes and myths of Brahma into his metaphysical relationship with the Infinite. <header>Brah —</header>

**Brahma**, he along with **Vishnu** and **Shiva**, are not the Infinite itself, but the Infinite is within them. 18. <note>This refers to the *Trimurti* (the Great Trinity), where the three gods represent different aspects of the one ultimate reality, or *Brahman*.</note>

# Shiva —

**Shiva**, whose symbols are the bull, the Ganges, the trident, the Lingam, and the Yoni. See there. <note>The Lingam and Yoni are sacred symbols in Hinduism representing the masculine and feminine generative powers of the universe, respectively.</note>

Note 26. <note>In Hindu myth, the Ganges fell from heaven and was caught in Shiva's matted hair to soften its impact on the Earth, signifying his role as a sustainer of life.</note>

— he is enthroned on the heavenly mountain Mahameru with the tablet of all the secrets of the Divine and the whole world. 38. **Leibniz’s** explanation of the mysterious expressions Li, Tai-ki, Shang-ti or Xang-ti among the Chinese. <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was deeply interested in Chinese philosophy, particularly the Neo-Confucian concepts of *Li* (principle), *Taiji* (the Supreme Ultimate), and *Shangdi* (the Supreme Deity), which he attempted to reconcile with European Christian theology.</note> Vol. II, p. 197 and following.

**Pitripett.** Vol. I, p. 191. <note>This likely refers to Pitripaksha, the Hindu period dedicated to performing rituals for ancestors (Pitrs).</note>

**Planets**, presented as under-kings of heaven and mediators for humanity. Vol. II, p. 45.

**Plantain.** See **Bananas.**

**Plantano.** See **Bananas.**

**Plithana** or **Pluthana**, a city of ancient India. Vol. III, pp. 140, 142. <note>Plithana is an ancient inland market town mentioned in the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*, often identified with modern-day Paithan.</note>

**Poetry**; Asian poetry judged. Vol. I, pp. 257–259.

**Polier** (the Chief) shows the Indian preparation of Rose-Attar. Vol. III, pp. 277 and following. <note>Antoine Polier (1741–1795) was a Swiss-born adventurer, engineer, and scholar who collected Persian and Sanskrit manuscripts. "Rose-Attar" (Ittar) is the highly concentrated essential oil extracted from rose petals.</note>

**Pollear.** Vol. I, p. 172. Vol. II, pp. 221–223. See **Ganesa.** <note>Pollear is a phonetic rendering of "Pillaiyar," a common Tamil name for the elephant-headed deity Ganesha.</note>

**Prah** or **Prah Pudi Djan**, that is, the Saint of high descent; a name for **Sammonakhodom.** See this word. <note>"Prah" is a Thai honorific (Phra) used for gods, kings, and monks. "Pudi Djan" likely refers to *Putthichao* (Buddha-lord).</note>

**Prah Khdi**, name of the teaching and prayer house of the monks and priests of Sammonakhodam. Vol. III, p. 444. <note>Sammonakhodam is an early European transcription of the Thai name for Gautama Buddha (*Sommonokhodom*). "Prah Khdi" refers to a *Kuti*, the living quarters or cells for monks within a Buddhist monastery (*Wat*).</note>

**Praleya**. Vol. II, p. 228. <note>In Hindu cosmology, *Pralaya* refers to the periodic dissolution of the universe at the end of a cosmic cycle.</note>

— the Siamese and Sinhalese do not have a specific caste for them. Vol. III, p. 445.

**Priestley** asks: whether phlogistic matter might not be the most essential part of the nourishment and preservation of both plants and animals? and Ad. Burt affirms this. Vol. III, p. 267. <note>Joseph Priestley (1733–1804) was a British chemist who discovered oxygen but remained a proponent of the "phlogiston" theory, which suggested a fire-like element resided within combustible bodies. **Pritu**, an ancient sage of India. Vol. III, p. 174. <note>Refers to King Prithu, a legendary monarch from the Puranas who is said to have "milked" the Earth to provide food and medicine for humanity.</note>

**Ptolemy** on the location of the ancient city Tagara. Vol. III, p. 143. <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Alexandrian geographer. Tagara was an important ancient inland trade center in the Deccan, identified with modern-day Ter.</note>

**Pukhto** or **Pushto**, name of the Afghan language. Vol. I, pp. 312, 314.

**Pulasakti**, son of Capardin and Mahadeva. Vol. III, p. 152. <note>Likely referring to Pulastya, one of the mind-born sons of Brahma. "Mahadeva" (The Great God) and "Capardin" (The One with Matted Hair) are both epithets of the god Shiva.</note>

**Punah**, the residence of the Maratha Peshwa. Vol. III, p. 367. <note>Modern-day Pune, which was the seat of the Peshwas, the de facto hereditary prime ministers of the Maratha Empire.</note>

**Punjabi language**. Vol. III, p. 466.

**Punjabhumt**, "The Land of Virtues," as the Indians call their land. Vol. I, p. 5. <note>original: "Punjabhumt"</note> <note>A transcription of *Punya-bhumi*, the Sanskrit term for "The Sacred Land" or "Land of Spiritual Merit," often used to describe the Indian subcontinent.</note>

**Punjaleh** or **Pumialeh**, a fruit. Vol. III, pp. 90, 473.

<header>II. Index for the first three volumes</header>

**Purana**, name of Indian scriptures and commentaries on all sorts of subjects regarding religion, law, etc. Vol. I, p. 32. <note>The Puranas are a vast genre of Indian literature about a wide range of topics, particularly legends and traditional lore.</note>
— the 18 excellent ones of **Vyasa**. Vol. I, p. 282. <note>Vyasa is the legendary sage to whom the authorship of the 18 "Great" (*Maha*) Puranas is traditionally attributed.</note>

**Purandhar**, a primary fortress of the Marathas. Vol. III, p. 371. <note>A historic hill fort in Maharashtra, India, which played a significant role in the history of the Maratha Empire.</note>

**Purriksh**, name of an Indian ordeal. Vol. II, p. 243 ff. <note>Likely referring to *Pariksha*, a system of judicial trials by ordeal used in ancient and medieval India to determine guilt or innocence.</note>

**Put**, also **Po**, **Fo**, that is, **Buddha**. Vol. III, pp. 30, 31, 43. <note>These are early European attempts to reconcile the various names for the Buddha across different Asian languages: *Put* (from Malay/Thai), *Po* and *Fo* (from Chinese).</note>

**Puticaraja**, Sanskrit name of a plant. Vol. III, p. 385. <note>Typically refers to the *Guilandina bonduc* or "fever nut" plant, used in traditional medicine.</note>

**Pyramids**, the Indian (quite similar to the Egyptian) were, according to R. Burrow, originally mere representations of **Mahadeo** or **Mahadeva**. Vol. III, pp. 188–189. <note>Reuben Burrow (1747–1792) was a mathematician and surveyor who speculated on the connections between ancient cultures. Here he suggests that Hindu temple towers (*Shikharas*) and pyramids were both symbols of the god Shiva (Mahadeva).</note>

**Raghu**, son of Buddha as **Shakya**. Vol. III, p. 249. See **Shakya**. <note>The text here reflects early, sometimes confused, Western attempts to link the solar dynasty of King Raghu with the lineage of Gautama Buddha (the Shakyamuni).</note>

**Raghunath Rao**, called **Raghoba**, murders his nephew **Narayan Rao**; his usurpation, his character. Vol. III, pp. 366–376 ff. <note>Raghunath Rao was a Peshwa (prime minister) of the Maratha Empire whose internal family struggles and alliance with the British led to the First Anglo-Maratha War.</note>

**Primitive reason of all things** <note>original: "*Raison primitive de toutes choses*"</note> of the Chinese according to **Leibniz**. Vol. II, pp. 195–196. <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) sought to find common ground between European philosophy and the Chinese concept of *Li* (principle or reason).</note>

**Rakhshe**, a miraculous beast of **Hoshang** with 12 feet. Vol. II, pp. 94–95. <note>Hoshang is a legendary king from the Persian *Shahnameh*. The "Rakhshe" is likely a reference to a mythical creature or a specific horse, though "12 feet" suggests a fabulous animal description found in early Orientalist accounts.</note>

**Rama**. Vol. I, pp. 16, 44.
— as **Dionysus**. Vol. I, p. 218 ff. <note>Early British scholars, like Sir William Jones, often compared the Hindu deity Rama to the Greek god Dionysus as part of "comparative mythology."</note>
— the 7th Avatar of **Vishnu**, his era. Vol. I, p. 377.

# Table XVIII.b.

<note>This table serves as a linguistic bridge, comparing the consonants of the Sanskrit language as written in two different systems: the Devanagari script (used primarily in Northern India) and the Telugu script (used in Southern India). The symbols are arranged phonetically, grouped by where the sound is produced in the mouth.</note>

| Sanskrit (Devanagari Script) | Telugu Script Equivalent |
|---|---|
| <term>ṅa</term> <note>original: ङ; a nasal sound made at the back of the throat, like the "ng" in "sing".</note> | <term>ṅa</term> <note>original: ఙ</note> |
| <term>ca</term> <note>original: च; a palatal sound, like the "ch" in "church".</note> | <term>ca</term> <note>original: చ</note> |
| <term>cha</term> <note>original: छ; an aspirated "ch" sound, pronounced with a sudden burst of air.</note> | <term>cha</term> <note>original: ఛ</note> |

*sna dgna cr dgia tnabdab dha rna tta gma kshma*
സ്ന ദഗ്ന ക്ര ദ്യ തബ്ദബ്ധ ർന്ന ത്ത ഗ്മ ക്ഷ്മ

# Final "broken" letters <note>Original Latin: "Litterae Finales fractae." These are known as *chillu* letters in Malayalam—consonants that are "broken" because they do not have an inherent vowel sound and stand alone at the end of a syllable.</note>

## Consonants

## Broken Final Letters.
<note>original: "Litterae Finales fractae"</note>

<note>A single row of terminal consonant forms, known in Malayalam as "Chillu" letters. These are specialized versions of consonants used when the sound is "broken" or "final"—meaning the consonant is pronounced purely on its own without the inherent "a" vowel sound that usually follows it.</note>
